title: Differential width discrimination task for active and passive tactile discrimination in humans
author: Perrotta, Pais-Vieira, et al.

steps.title: Obtain consent and prepare participant
steps.instruction: Verify that the subject has signed the informed‑consent form, fit the EEG cap if required, and seat the subject comfortably in front of the frontal panel (CFP) with the push‑button panel and lighting system ready.

steps.title: Measure finger size in CFP
steps.instruction: Ask the subject to place the index finger in the CFP, then slowly move the two bars inward from each side until the subject reports that the bars are touching the finger and exerting pressure on the distal interphalangeal joint; record the distance between the bars and subtract 1.0–2.0 mm to obtain the calibrated finger size used for aperture calculations.

steps.title: Configure aperture widths for task version
steps.instruction: Set the variable‑aperture width according to the task version: for active runs, set the wide aperture to finger size + 0.5 cm and the narrow aperture to finger size + 0.0 cm; for passive runs, set the wide aperture to finger size + 0.2 cm and the narrow aperture to finger size − 0.2 cm. These values can be adjusted later if other experimental variables are studied.

steps.title: Run practice trials
steps.instruction: Before placing the EEG cap, give the subject a short practice session consisting of 15 trials of each condition (active‑wide, active‑narrow, passive‑wide, passive‑narrow) so they become familiar with the instructions and the timing of the lights and buttons.

steps.title: Execute experimental runs
steps.instruction: Perform four experimental runs. Each run contains 20 trials (10 wide, 10 narrow) pseudo‑randomized to avoid consecutive identical stimuli. Alternate the runs between passive and active versions (e.g., Run 1 = passive, Run 2 = active, Run 3 = passive, Run 4 = active).

steps.title: Conduct individual trial sequence
steps.instruction: For each trial follow these actions in order:

substeps.instruction: Center light turns yellow → subject places finger in the CFP.
Algorithm detects correct finger position → center light turns green.
Allow the subject to sample the aperture for 500 ms. In active trials the subject may move the finger; in passive trials the bars move toward the stationary finger.
Center light turns red → subject removes the finger and presses the corresponding push button (wide or narrow).
Four‑LED display shows ‘correct’ or ‘incorrect’ and updates the total number of correct responses.
Inter‑trial interval of 500 ± 50 ms signaled by the center light turning red again; the subject must keep the finger out of the CFP during this interval.

steps.title: Record responses and finish session
steps.instruction: Log the button choice, correctness, and reaction times for every trial; after the fourth run, save all data files and remove the EEG cap (if used).

description: The present research protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Universidade do Minho (SECVS 148/2016; and the Ethics Committee of the Universidade Católica Portuguesa (39/2017), according to the Code of Ethics of the World Medical Association (Declaration of Helsinki) for experiments involving humans. All participating subjects voluntarily filled an informed consent. Due to the methodological nature of the present manuscript we will only present results from a reduced number of subjects (n = 9) that were tested with the goal of exploring the upper and lower bounds of the task, namely: number of trials, intertrial intervals, session duration, trial duration, active and passive discrimination limits, effects of different versions of the task in EEG recordings. In Fig. 4, we present the behavioral results for a single subject performing the width discrimination task with multiple levels of difficulty (two sessions for each distance). In the active version of the task, the highest performances (>70%) were found for 0.3 cm. When the distances were smaller than 0.15 cm the performances in the active version of the task dropped to near chance levels. When the subject was tested in the passive version of the task, a maximum of 96% correct responses was found for distances of 0.3 cm. As the difference between the two apertures became smaller than 0.1 cm, the performance in the passive version of the task dropped to near chance levels. These results suggested that – in the present set of distances tested – the passive version of the task presented increased performances for larger distances when compared to the active version of the task. Meanwhile, both versions presented low performances when small distances were tested.
